A few months ago, we revisited Intel's user-facing drivers (including Arc Control) to see how they'd improved over one year of patches. Now, we're benchmarking the Intel Arc lineup in more depth to see how they compete with NVIDIA and AMD graphics cards in 2024. These Intel Arc GPU benchmarks include the A770, A750, A580, and A380 video cards vs. the RTX 4060, RX 6600 and 6600 XT, RX 7600, 7600 XT, and more. We're seeking to answer whether Intel Arc is any good (yet), and specifically, how it competes in the value side of the market with AMD. Large parts of this video will be simple discussion about the interesting way this battle is playing out: Namely, with AMD and Intel fighting over the modern "low end" while NVIDIA leaves it relatively untouched with new parts.

just a suggestion, tossing Quake 2 RTX to the list isnt a horrible idea, it works amazingly on the a770 last i tested i did have to enable a toggle to get the perf up but, that may be a default now its been a while, either way, it also looks amazing for a game from my youth that shipped with both software and accelerated rendering support... better then some modern games... (also, we will be seeing more projects like this as nv have released that kit/project to replace the renderer in old games with one capable of modern features.. ) 

when we tested it was shocking how well it ran, better then the 3060ti despite it being older drivers from around this time last year now that we went and looked at when we did the tests... 

another suggestion if you see this.. a video showing arc on a range of cpu's and games to figure out where the sweet spot is.. 

again i get better results at 1440p and 4k in some of these titles then your benches are showing, and am on a much older cpu.. 7980xe, that i am regularly reminded "isnt a gaming cpu"...in the intel chat... by ppl who think a 5700g would have been  better buy for around the same price..heh..) 

i do know its alot of work, but it could just be the 770 16g cards for the first run and if it looks interesting enough run the other cards, im betting the cut off for cpu will be quite a range depending on the games you play,  then you will hit a point where you have enough cores/threads to deal with the cpu doing the "scorebording"  for the gpu and still being in the process of heavy optimization,  from our testing though a 7900x@5ghz with an acer a770 gets noicably better results on some titles vs his 12700h+a770m Nuc, where a few titles do run better on the nuc, its marginal most of of the time... and a few titles really hate the mixed-core chips and need you to force them to only use p cores.. using process lasso or similar.. 

anyway good video, i would say these are already aging better then nvidia products they compete against.. not 100% of the time but.. getting closer and closer.... and amd's 7600xt has the same issue as the 4060ti 16gb.. buss limitations, even at 1440p it starts to show.. and thats honestly arcs "Sweet spot" most of the time... sometimes its still faster at 1440p then 1080p... thats down to both drivers and hardware design, i think they might do well to hurry and get a DSR/VSR style toggle in drivers so people on 1080p screens could run at 1440p...thats the ONE feature i genuinely f-ing miss from amd and nvidia drivers... nvidias handling is better but... i just want a downscaling toggle... having to use crap like cru to try and do this shite is just.. frustrating and irritating.. heh..

comments.text:
One very important part to test on Arc are indeed DX11 and DX9 games.
Intel put performance in pre DX12 APIs aside, and performance suffered as expected. And many especially esports oriented games still run on these older APIs, and injectors like DXVK aren't an option.
They are priced in the midrange, basically where people who play esports and older titles would more likely grab a card.

Over here as of now (early April 2024)
 - A380 around 130 €
 - A580 around 190 €
 - A750 around 220 €
 - RX 6600 around 220 €
 - RX 7600 around 280 €
 - RTX 3060 around 290 €
 - RTX 4060 around 315 €
 - A770 around 330-350 €
 - RX 7600 XT around 360 €
 - RTX 4060 Ti around 400 €

With those prices and re performance results the A580 and A750 will give great performance for the money, the A750 clocking in roughly at the same price as a RX 6600, but much better performance.
But the real winner is the RX 7600. Priced similar to the RTX 3060, but vastly outperforms it.

The RTX 3060 is a clear loser. Costs as much as a RX 7600, but performs like a RX 6600. In 2024 the RTX 4060 is clearly a much better card, both in performance and performance for money. Price difference is rather small, but worth the step up.

The A770 is priced between the 4060 on one side and the 7600 XT on the other, but performs closer to the 4060. At that point, just get a 7600 XT, unless raytracing is important, at which point the 4060 will perform much better and at a lower price.

The RX 7600 XT itself costs a lot for it's performance. Both the A770 and 4060 Ti will give a better price/performance ratio.

So at this point in 2024 I would recommend the A750, RX 7600 and RTX 4060, each in their own price bracket at 190€, 220€, 280€ and 315€
I would stay away from the A380 (just too slow for anything), RTX 3060 (too expensive for it's performance) and RX 7600 XT (also too expensive for it's performance)

That is for gaming. for video decoding the A380 is really great low cost option.

comments.text:
I love your videos but I don't like when these videos describe "anything below 60FPS average" as "unplayable."

It's not factual. (Obviously, to me and you! But some viewers are kids just watching this, or folks who haven't owned a gaming PC ever or for decades, may be watching this before making their next purchase. And for whatever reason, viewers may not have the necessary frame of reference to understand this is a figure of speech and not literally true.) Some are riding it out on a lower-end rig and are watching this as enthusiasts. Being an enthusiast should be no-purchase-necessary, and calling the gameplay they're getting "unplayable" is kind of insulting, yet without really adding to the discussion. There should be no "you must be this rich, or must buy hardware this often, to play" to be an enthusiast and enjoy watching these videos.

It's potentially insulting to some viewers. 30FPS gamers aren't going anywhere. Who even wins when describing gameplay like this? It's not accurate enough to be usable as buying advice, or even as a relative performance thing, given the 0 attention paid to 1% lows when marking this arbitrary cutoff point. Buying low-spec rigs on purpose is valid if you know what you're doing, trying to get a little gaming in on a computer that's not a dedicated gaming PC is valid, riding out on an older rig while waiting to make a new purchase is valid. Therefore, 30FPS gaming is valid. Full stop.

It's imprecise and confusing. Consider these parts of the video: 1) where you said the 750 and 770 and AMD were all "unplayable," but that Arc "kept up better than AMD does." Like, if they are "unplayable", why are you still comparing their performance? (Because it shows how well the cards do relatively, I get it, but you see how confusing that sounds, right?) 2) You also called out a game with ~62FPS avg but 52FPS lows as being "playable ... but maybe just barely" depending on gamers' preferences... while on a different graph calling a game where Arc A380 had ~59FPS avg and 30FPS lows as "in an absolute sense ... playable at the very least". That much of a discrepancy between average and 1% lows, is to me, not something I would put up with. Attempting to give a caveat there in the phrasing, to stretch the meaning of "playable" so it still applies, is such a huge stretch, IMO. I am left wondering: why try to "make it work" and save this arbitrary metric to be able to apply it, when it doesn't really mean anything? The ">= 60FPS avg means playable" metric is a really supremely bad metric. It encourage oversimplification based on averages, to the neglect of frametime stability or really anything else.

I don't know about you, but I'd happily take something where the 1% lows are above 50FPS and decently close to the averages, over something where the 1% lows are only half of the average FPS...! I mean, honestly, what does "playable" even mean at this point, really? 1% lows being half the average is to me so much more of a dealbreaker, but they're equal under this "playable" terminology.

Please do consider dropping this terminology of "playable" meaning "60FPS average FPS and up" from your content. IMHO, it's even worse than saying nothing that characterizes how nice the experience is at all. IMO, it's just that imprecise and just does not add to the conversation positively, only adds confusion because it's being used so loosely.

I would strongly suggest saying something else, like maybe "it's rough" playing at this framerate, or "it might be a dealbreaker for some viewers" or "it's not as nice if you're used to higher FPS". Anything that meaningfully indicates how the experience might be and is still truthful and accurate, unlike "playable" / "not playable" outside of game-breaking bugs. If "it's rough" doesn't apply, then maybe hold back dismissing sub-60FPS gameplay out of hand. If it's not that bad, don't call it unplayable then.

And seriously consider thinking about the lows too if you're characterizing how nice an experience the game is going to be. 59FPS average at 32FPS 1% lows is most likely not a better experience. Gamers will experience 1% low frametimes more than once per two seconds of gameplay, on average. That level of inconsistency, dropping to half-FPS stutters more than once every two seconds, would be much more of a dealbreaker for me personally than, say, 45FPS gameplay with 40FPS lows. As long as it's consistent, IMO, it's pretty well playable down to maybe a 24FPS cut-off point, at least for me personally.

Higher FPS is nicer, if it's steady. Heck, any gameplay at all is a blessing if it's steady, IMO, at about 24FPS+. Otherwise, give me a framerate limiter and 30FPS for rock-solid framerates any day, over uneven gameplay with higher "averages." Stutters break immersion. You can't even tell what FPS you're looking at in low-motion content, and give it a few minutes and you'll adjust to lower FPS for the higher-motion pans and high-action scenes. Not as nice, but you get used to it. On the other hand, extreme stutters away from the average are awful at any FPS, IMO. It kinda depends on your monitor, too, but don't most people still own 60FPS displays? Lows matter so much more on 60FPS displays. Anything past 60 isn't even viewable on those displays or you'll get tearing.

I own a machine that gets well above 60FPS in all the games I play, and still I do a double-take every time I hear such a thorough reviewer as your channel say "playable" vs "unplayable" with such strong language, only to basically indicate "a single stat went higher than an arbitrary cutoff point" -- like, come on. That's not meaningful nor accurate. It's also unfactual.

So, to wrap up: I don't know how we got here, where the top reviewers seem to have standardized on something that, IMO, falls below a professional standard. It's not a helpful way to explain how nice a game is to play.

I already gave HardwareUnboxed a hard time in the comments of one of their videos about this. This video's use of the term really seemed egregious, IMO, so I felt I had to share my view to your channel's comments as well.

Once again, I really appreciate your content. It helps me understand the PC market a ton better than I ever would, and I learn new things about games and hardware all the time from this channel. Thank you for considering this feedback.

Best Regards.

comments.text:
I'm just hoping that Battlemage will both still come out before it's moot (it went from speculated April/May of this year to maybe sometime in 2025, if at all), and it will be able to take advantage of the driver improvements for this line in some way or another. I've been sitting with a 6800 XT for a while because nothing else offers enough to be worth the extra cost IMO. Games wise the most demanding title I play is cyberpunk, and even then I usually run 1080 windowed on a 3440x1440 main display. At that resolution, I can easily push all the settings and be fine in terms of power demand. Full screen 1440p (not ultrawide, aspect ratio preserved) with minor upscaling I can still run full blast and it looks great (and that will only get better as upscaling improves).

Speaking of upscaling, that's another factor that will help Intel in the long run, IMO. Between them improving their two version of upscaling (their better option being with ARC cards) and AMD's R&D that's opensource, their lower power cards will still be able to punch above their weight with the upscaling tech that's a LOT easier to deploy than nvidia's that requires more work for the developer. Even if nvidia's route produces better results, and it does for sure, the marginal increase isn't worth the added complexity. Arguably the same can be said for something like a 6800XT lasting even longer. I've been testing my budget setup with a Ryzen 2600, RX580 8GB gpu, and 16gb of ram. With upscaling that the RX580 8GB card supports, you can get really solid results for what it is. People will still buy cards to swing around like epeens with benchmark numbers, but for most people just playing games on a reasonable budget, upscaling is going to one of the biggest game changers going along with more budget friendly cards with the faster/larger amount of vram and processing that handle upscaling better than cheap old cards.

All AMD has to do is be more aggressive on pricing of its gpu's, the vast bulk of gpu's are from low to mid-end, where AMD is competitive in, the problem is its pricing structure isn't that compelling for most consumers, yes it's a bit cheaper than what Nvidia offers but it's also a worse product, AMD isn't gaining market share and in fact has been losing market share in the gpu market because it's not willing to do what's needed to gain market share, AMD were more aggressive on the cpu market, and it's been paying off.

Should also point out that AMD doesn't need to beat Nvidia on quality or performance, it's got a good enough line-up of gpu's that it can steal market share from Nvidia if it were more aggressive on pricing to actually temps us, unfortunately, the price being a little cheaper isn't encouraging many of us to switch.

It's where Intel could shake the market up once it sorts it's drivers are, which are in a much better state then a few years ago, assuming Intel pushes along with ARC 2 and 3 and are more aggressive in wanting to gain market share, which AMD doesn't seem to be, I feel that Intel will squeeze AMD from the bottom up because most consumers that buy AMD products, buy them without any real loyalty because they want a product that's cheaper, that makes AMD an easy target for Intel, as long as you have a decent product and are far more aggressive on pricing then AMD wants to be, they will steal market share in the low to mid-end market.

As for Nvidia, it's going to take a lot more to beat them, they have the market share and mind share, they also have the better product on the market, but the truth is, most of the market is low to mid-end, not high end, AMD is already competitive on performance in the low and mid-end, but not on pricing, Intel is on the low end but needs more work in the mid-end.

Personally, I feel Intel can reshape the gpu market a lot more than AMD can, and not because Intel has a lot more resources to play with but because Intel doesn't fear Nvidia, in fact, Intel doesn't like Nvidia and won't want to play second fiddle to them, in other words, Intel will likely be far more aggressive on pricing and gaining market share then AMD is, and honestly, I can't help but feel that AMD and Nvidia are in it together with fixing the gpu market and pricing, I mean, AMD have been far more aggressive on the cpu market but on gpu's, it's like they are trying to not compete with Nvidia, and fair enough they can't compete with Nvidia at the top end on performance, but they can be far more aggressive on pricing to win us over.

The funny thing is, I've been an AMD fanboy for so long that I'm starting to give up on AMD, they don't seem to have what's needed or the will needed to shake up the gpu market, Intel, if they deliver on ARC 2 or 3, will likely be my next gpu upgrade.

comments.text:
A few months ago (my original comment was 7 months ago, so a few months after that). I decided to sell my 6700XT to a friend to help their build, and use that to buy an Arc A750. Ideally I'd have gotten a 770 but frankly I'm not too concerned about the performance drop. And I will be replacing it with Intel's next generation GPU. I really just wanted the box and GPU as a sort of celebration of Intel's first real GPU.

I've been using the Arc 750 for a few months, and I have essentially no issues with any of my games. And performance issues I'm pretty sure are just from it being a lower-end card, and are solved by dropping the resolution.
I also recently moved over entirely to Linux for my gaming PC. Also no isues. You'd think the combination of both Linux compatibility layers and a weird GPU would be a problem, but they aren't. Intel's driver support is quite good. I don't even install Intel's driver software, I just update my OS and it gets drivers.

So yeah, Arc's going great for me. I'm sure if I was a more demanding gamer, playing all the newest games, it'd be a problem. But I'm not that so all good.

Honestly the real issue is the Intel CPU (i5-12400). There are a number of games that need fixes (in both Windows and Linux) because Intel left some bugs in these CPUs. Titanfall 2 for example wont connect to multiplayer without a weird launch command (minor inconvenience, but annoying). An indie game called Forza Polpo crashes because it's on an old Unity build that runs into the hardware bug. It's very minor but I never heard about this issue online so I wanted to highlight it. No clue if newer Intel CPUs solve this or not.

comments.text: @chaos3088  It is a bit of a weird card. 1080p OK, 1440p better and 4k it can do things that 4070ti can't. There are growing number of XeSS XMX supported games +70. 4k mid and high settings playable and if XeSS XMX supported it does pretty well. Because ARC has very good frame time you really can't compare FPS alone. For example if you get 50-60FPS on 4k to match it with 4070ti you need 100FPS if not more. Plus 192 bus from the 4070ti is not enough. ARC has 256 bus that gives lot better 4k performance. 4070ti has to be said is better at 1440p. AMD/Nvidia does most of the executions in the GPU where Wattage matters. For example if we use 4070ti as an example it is 285W GPU. INTEL ARC A770 is 225W GPU but you need to count the CPU in with it. The task is split between GPU and CPU and them brought together to minimize queuing to give better frame time. Less FPS is needed for the same performance. This is why more you demand closer the gap gets to more expensive cards. Don't get me wrong it has driver issues but so does AMD and Nvidia. INTEL is not that far behind anymore and if I would rate gaming at the older games you can do most of the popular games and almost all of the new and XeSS XMX support just keeps on growing. As coding and workstation card the ARC is excellent and to get better you would have to pay $1000. But make sure you are running a high end INTEL platform where it works the best. AMD platform seems it is getting left behind as the drivers mature and the GPU is starting to take it full potential. My prediction is that it has 20% still on the table and maybe more when APO (Application Optimization) starts to become a thing that seems to promise 10-50% performance boost. I think this will come with Battlemage and more common with Celestial. But with 14th gen CPU it should also lift the Alchemist. Lot happening.

comments.text:
This reminds me of the olden days of 1998-1999 when S3 was trying to get somewhere between ATI, 3dfx, Matrox and NVIDIA. It was the old 2D powerhouse that had become the underdog of the early 3D era. Their price-cut Savage 4 had a place in my heart for having given my pocket-money-wielding teenage self access to some 3D PC gaming despite its quirks. They did have a clear edge in texture quality for games supporting S3TC, such as Unreal Tournament. S3TC was later renamed to DXTC as Microsoft made it standard in DirectX. I was really rooting for S3 to break through with the Savage 2000 back then, the only other graphics card to feature hardware T&L like the first GeForce, but it was a flop due to very poor drivers. They got bought by VIA who ended up only using their technology for chipset integrated graphics.

Anyway, ramblings of an old guy aside, I hope that Intel finds its place and climbs the ladder to challenge NVIDIA. We need some serious competition, not only on the graphics side, but also the AI side.

comments.text:
I think it differs from game to game, also some glitches are just temporary. The only rendering differences you'll usually spot are between XeSS and DLSS. Some glitches are part of the in-game rendering that gets smoothed out by TAA by default, and XeSS isn't handling them properly. The Starfield problem is the game itself, there were render problems on other hardware at launch and Intel is largely left to do their own testing (developer in-house testing gear is unlikely to include ARC). Intel is starting to do a better job at having "launch day" drivers for new games implying they at least get advanced copies of new games to test.

While it's possible that reasons for driver issues could be spotted in testing, I don't think it's very plausible. Driver issues can be very simple but they can take weeks, months, or years to track down. NVidia still has issues for multimonitor users that have lasted a decade.

But your point about XeSS vs DLSS vs FSR... using TAA across all tests, or running pure native would be ideal for this test to differentiate anything specific to that game's utilization of resources. I'm curious if even DLSS would run smoother than XeSS in some cases with ARC.

comments.text:
@CTYCompRepair  I don't know if "pure native" is something you're going to want to use with most titles. You can turn TAA off in CP2077 for instance (there's a config file where you insert some text), it looks a bit like a mirror ball and needs TAA to make the game playable. Having DLSS/DLAA as an option would be nice to try but I'd rather see the latest version of XeSS in more games, it's quite good.

I do think it's an issue that FSR doesn't have a similar quality level to DLSS or XeSS, it makes comparison more difficult. I've only used FSR and XeSS at 1080p (FSR with NVidia and AMD) and XeSS is just way more usable, even at "balanced" settings. There's a bit of performance unutilized at 1080p, at least on my rig, so I get similar FPS at "quality" or higher. At 1440p you don't get that problem (although 1440p is probably the limit for these GPUs with current gen games).

This is not something I've tested myself but something I've heard  from someone else...

The idea was getting better performance in video handling and compressing. The user bought a A310 ARC card and added it to his gaming machine that was running a i5-13600K and a Nvidia RTX-3070. After installing the A310, not connecting a monitor to it, he disabled the graphics integrated into the i5-13600K. The videosoftware that was previously using the quick sync technology would now use the A310 instead of the graphics processor in the CPU. According to what I was told the addition of the A310 increased the encoding performance drastically.

Now this is an interesting idea if it actually works. A AMD user might be able to use Quick Sync when handling video encode and such. Or users of Intel processors that doesn't have the integrated GPU might be able to enhance their machines performance.

comments.text:
@canaconn2388  
RX-5000 is just an abbreviation for AMD's first-gen RDNA graphics. It was a fairly substantial increase in terms of value and efficiency. But it didn't catch up to Nvidia's pervious generation GTX cards in terms of performance. Nor the current RTX cards in terms of performance. It was only a good thing for the midrange market, but not so for the high-end or luxury segments.

RTX-2 is just abbreviation to say the Nvidia RTX-2000 series. That came with no performance uplift, but a price bump, trying to justify its new feature-set (AI and Ray Tracing). It was the start of the end.

The RTX-3 is an abbreviation for Nvidia's RTX-3000 series. It looked like a massive uplift, only because the RTX-2 series wasn't. If you compared it on a graph, you would've realised it was NOT impressive compared to the GTX-10 series when plotted against time. At least it came with a smaller price bump, and a decent efficiency uplift. However, because Nvidia had been SO MUCH complacent it allowed AMD to catch up. The early RX-6800 and RX-6800Xt cards hold up VERY well even today, but their direct priced competitors from Nvidia like the RTX-3060Ti, 3070, 3070Ti they are struggling today. They have to dial down performance either from 120fps to 60fps, or Max Settings to High, or from 2160p/1440p down to 1440p/1080p resolution. Primarily the VRAM limitation, but also Nvidia reducing their software updates to it. For that reason, the RX-6800 is the true successor to the GTX-1080Ti when it comes to the Smart Shopper.

Sorry this was a VERY LONG post, and I reached out to Tech Jesus, because I think Steve is more knowledgeable than I am and he would be able to make a much better content than I am.

comments.text:
@dead-claudia   Not really.

There is a reason AMD basically put it's GPU division on life support for what, like 5 years? Something like that - and it was trying to catch up to NVIDIA and break into that market as a competitor was basically impossible. Even if trying to compete on price - NVIDIA historically just shuffled their prices a bit and people bought NVIDIA regardless of how good the current AMD/ATI cards were - which is more or less how AMD ended up buying ATI. So AMD focused REALLY HEAVILY on CPU's, and that is the Zen Architecture.

Over the last several years, AMD has been focused largely on fixing the driver experience, improving feature parity, and so on - and they are ALMOST there: Not perfect, but a lot of stuff is "good enough" and what needs done more than anything is refinement.

AMD is now in a really good spot for their ability to put money into R&D, and it's fixing some of the internal design philosophy, refining technologies, and finding architecture choices that will really matter. That does not happen over night - but ultimately: AMD will be fine.

Now - lets look at the Integrated Graphics that we are starting to see from both AMD and Intel: That is the story we should be talking about - because like it or not, if you can buy a CPU, motherboard, ram, power supply, and an M.2 drive, slot it all together - and you have a computer that is "good enough" for low to mid range graphics output at 60ish fps - that is a HUGE change in dynamic for getting into PC gaming, and with AMD and Intel drivers being the default - people will stop looking at NVIDIA as the default go to - and instead, start becoming more confident and comfortable with either AMD or Intel based solutions which means: NVIDIA within a few years may not be able to rely on their Mind Share Fortress. This should all happen at roughly a time line where AMD and Intel are catching up in overall performance, power efficiency, and so on with new architectures.

The reality is: NVIDIA paved the way for a lot of things, and has a comfortable safe place in the market for decades at this point - but that is likely to change. There is a reason NVIDIA has been hell bent on AI accelerators and focused on Enterprise solutions: The writing has been on the wall for half a decade at this point with Intel needing to be lead by an Engineer to solve their issues that AMD breaking into the CPU market caused them, and the reality is - Intel has had several dGPU projects over the years that got mothballed by Bean Counters and Marketing departments that also happened to starve the R&D of the resources they needed in favor of Stock Holder Dividend Payouts - But Intel is on the hunt now. And I am excited.

So ya: AMD is going to be pressured to clean up some issues - which is good for everyone. But the real party that is going to need to be concerned in the coming years is NVIDIA. The truth is: AMD and Intel have the design chops to get a different architecture CPU out the door - I mean hell, Most CISC (as in x86 CPU's) are cores that are a pile of specialized accelerators packaged together to handle different instructions - which is to say: Even if a new entrant architecture comes into play, AMD and Intel are poised to take a stab at it it's just, right now - there is no real market for it. For NVIDIA it's a whole different equation that they are trying to solve for.  So again: There is a reason NVIDIA has been so focused on the Enterprise space: It's where their future is.

And that Mobo(sans BIOS update), CPU instructions, and DDR3(32GB - 1600MHz Quad Core).

All of my high end screens are 1080p, so I don't need any upgrades for a 2-3 years.
I feel like the constant Intel driver updates make the performance better and better.
